cards.title: The Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg evasiveness conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For every integer n≥2 and every nonconstant function f from the simple undirected graphs on [n] to {0,1} that is invariant under every permutation of [n] and monotone under adding edges, is D(f)=n(n−1)/2, where D(f) is its deterministic worst-case adjacency-query complexity?
cards.why: This asks whether every nontrivial monotone graph property can force complete inspection of its adjacency data, even when all computation between queries is free. A resolution would identify an exact limit of adaptive information gathering imposed by graph symmetry.

progress.text: Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant, Theorem 1, establish exact evasiveness for every nontrivial monotone graph property when the number of vertices is a prime power.
Aaronson and coauthors, Theorem 5, prove the optimal universal Omega(n) bounded-error quantum query lower bound. This is a separate query model.
Elekes and coauthors, version 3, Section 1.1, retain the finite conjecture as open while studying failures of infinite-vertex extensions.

Benedetti’s CATA IV abstract announces a counterexample to topological evasiveness. No finite graph-property counterexample is specified in the abstract; the related author publication list still labels the manuscript in preparation at this review.

cards.definitions: Write [n]={1,…,n} and U_n={{i,j}:1≤i<j≤n}; a graph is an arbitrary edge set E⊆U_n, with no loops, parallel edges or input promises. Nonconstant means that f takes both values 0 and 1. Monotonicity means E⊆F implies f(E)≤f(F). Invariance means f(π(E))=f(E) for every permutation π of [n], where π(E)={{π(i),π(j)}:{i,j}∈E}. A deterministic query algorithm is a finite rooted binary decision tree. Each internal node names an unordered pair in U_n and its two outgoing edges correspond to the answer 0 or 1 for absence or presence of that pair; each leaf carries an output bit. Following the answers supplied by E must end with output f(E) for every E⊆U_n. The cost on E is the number of internal nodes visited, and D(f) is the minimum, over all such correct trees, of the maximum cost over E. Repeated queries can be omitted. The tree may depend arbitrarily on n and f; f is the fixed task, not an additional unknown input. Only queries count: computation, storage and the size of the tree are unrestricted, and no uniform procedure for constructing trees across n or f is required. The model is deterministic and exact, with no probability distribution over inputs. Reading every pair gives D(f)≤|U_n|.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove D(f)=|U_n| for every n and f satisfying the stated conditions, or refute this universal claim. A finite refutation consists of one n, a completely specified invariant nonconstant monotone f, and a correct decision tree whose depth is at most |U_n|−1. A lower bound only up to a constant factor, or a theorem restricted to particular properties or vertex counts, does not settle the full claim.

context_blocks.text: Imagine receiving a graph behind an interface that answers only whether a chosen pair of vertices is joined. The algorithm can choose its next pair after seeing earlier answers. The conjecture says that, for every qualifying property, even the best such strategy has some input on which it must inspect every possible pair.

For a concrete example, consider the property of having at least one edge. Finding an edge establishes a yes answer immediately. On the empty graph, however, every pair must be inspected: an unexamined pair could hide the only edge. Evasiveness is thus a worst-case requirement; it does not say that every graph forces a complete scan.

The hypotheses specify which questions qualify. A constant answer needs no queries, so it is excluded. Asking whether the particular pair {1,2} is an edge needs one query but depends on vertex labels, so it is excluded by isomorphism invariance. Monotonicity requires a yes answer to survive the addition of edges; connectivity and containing a triangle have this feature, whereas having exactly one edge does not.

Symmetry says that relabeling the graph cannot change the answer. It does not prevent the algorithm from using labels to decide which pair to inspect first. Moreover, the difficult input can depend on the algorithm. These distinctions make the conjecture much stronger than the observation that all edge positions are potentially relevant.

The older quadratic lower-bound question is settled. The remaining target is exact equality with the total number of pairs, including the last possible query. Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning n=p^k for a prime p and an integer k≥1. Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.

sentences: An algorithm learns an unknown graph by asking whether individual pairs of vertices are edges.
The conjecture asks whether every nonconstant monotone property invariant under vertex relabeling has some input requiring all possible pairs to be queried.
Queries may be adaptive and all computation between them is free.
The example of looking for one edge illustrates how an easy positive instance can coexist with an empty graph that requires a complete scan.

The exact claim is known for prime-power vertex counts, while results about quantum queries, infinite graphs and broader topological symmetry must be distinguished from the full finite deterministic question.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
